content: Yellow Jessamine, scientifically known as Gelsemium sempervirens, is a climbing vine belonging to the family Gelsemiaceae. It is native to warm temperate and tropical regions of the Americas, ranging from Guatemala to the southeastern United States. This plant can grow to a height of 3 to 6 meters when it has appropriate support, such as trees, to climb on. Its stems are thin, and the leaves are evergreen, lance-shaped, measuring 5 to 10 cm in length and 1 to 1.5 cm in width. The leaves are dark green and have a glossy appearance. The flowers of Yellow Jessamine grow in clusters. Each flower is trumpet-shaped, yellow in color, and sometimes features an orange center. The flowers are approximately 3 cm in length and 2.5 to 3 cm in width. All parts of this plant are toxic, as they contain strychnine-related alkaloids, specifically gelsemine and gelseminine. These compounds render the plant highly poisonous and unsuitable for consumption. Additionally, the plant's sap can cause skin irritation in individuals with heightened sensitivity. Children have been poisoned after mistaking the flowers for honeysuckle and consuming the nectar. The nectar itself is toxic to honeybees and can lead to brood death when collected by the bees. Despite these dangers, Yellow Jessamine remains a popular ornamental plant in warmer climates. It is often cultivated to grow over arbors or to cover walls. It is important to note that this flower lacks a scent, and its nectar is located at the base of the flower. Yellow Jessamine holds cultural significance as the state flower of South Carolina.
